job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in structural engineering at Hartwell Technical University, so mornings are lectures and afternoons are the design lab. I live in student housing, a corridor of eight rooms, and on Thursdays I cook pasta for the whole floor. My parents run a pharmacy in Dunmore and pay my fees, so I have no debt, and my brother Lucas is seventeen and still at school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like checking a beam by hand on a big sheet of paper before I trust the software. What wears me out is group projects where someone has a chatbot write the report and I fix it at midnight. I passed my bachelor's with an average result and never did an internship, and that still bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. In the design lab we joke that a chatbot can't check a load path, so my friends and I would just carry on. I might post one smug comment in the course group chat, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my plan holds. I finish the master's in June, get a graduate post at a bridge or building firm, and the pass degree matters less once I have the master's. Money isn't the worry, because my parents cover the fees and I have over six months of living costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my thesis on timber floors and apply to about fifteen structural firms around Dunmore and the city. I'd ask my supervisor Dr Weiss for a reference. I'd also try for a summer site placement, even unpaid, to make up for having no internship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, mostly. A bit guilty, too, that I feel so settled while my parents pay for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the missing internship bothers you. How much would it matter in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a little. Recruiters ask what I've built on site, and I've only built a balsa model footbridge. That's why I'd try for the placement even if nobody pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Lucas about studying engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Lucas to study engineering if he likes problems that have a right answer. I'd also tell him to join the student union early, because the union rep got me an extension when my laptop died.

say: I'd say that's what I expected, and a chatbot can't check a **load path**.
I'd tell friends to just **carry on** with their degrees.
think: My plan holds: finish the master's in June and land a **graduate post** at a structural firm.
Money isn't the worry, since my parents pay the fees and I have **six months saved**.
do: Finish my thesis on **timber floors** and apply to about fifteen structural firms.
Ask supervisor Dr Weiss for a reference and chase a summer **site placement**.
feel: Relaxed, though a bit **guilty** that my parents carry the cost.
S0.quote: I'd tell my brother Lucas to study engineering if he likes problems that have a right answer.
fieldNote: Settled because the money is covered; the only soft spot is **no internship**, which she raised unprompted.
Says her bluntest lines for friends and keeps her private plan modest and practical.

steps.text: Finish the master's thesis on timber floors by June
Apply to fifteen structural firms near Dunmore and the city
Keep the six months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies should be honest about which tasks they hand to software, and there should be rules. I'd say it at the union meeting and on the course forum. I wouldn't say I'm scared, because I'm not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the entry jobs are the checking and drafting jobs, and those are exactly what a graduate does first. Firms might take on two graduates instead of five. My family's money means I can wait, but I don't love that my average degree is no help in a smaller pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the master's and push my thesis towards something hands-on, like site inspection and old buildings. I'd ask Dr Weiss to put me on his bridge-monitoring project. I'd also join the graduate branch of the engineers' union and go to the first meeting in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job isn't gone, but the ladder looks shorter, and I think about it on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your course would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Priya has a good degree but she mostly copies from a chatbot. If firms test people on judgement, she might struggle, and if they test speed, I will. I worry for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. Does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I'd have to try one tool, and I'd pick the one the firm uses for load checks, so I can see its mistakes myself. I'd rather learn it to criticise it than to rely on it.

say: The companies should say which tasks go to software, and there should be **rules**.
I'd raise it at the union meeting rather than act scared.
think: Entry jobs are the **checking and drafting** jobs, so firms may hire two graduates instead of five.
My family's money lets me wait, but my **average degree** won't help in a smaller pile.
do: Steer my thesis towards **site inspection** and old buildings that software handles badly.
Join the graduate branch of the engineers' **union** and go in January.
feel: Uneasy, because the **career ladder** looks shorter than I planned.
S1.quote: Firms might take on two graduates instead of five.
fieldNote: Unease comes from the **shrinking entry rung**, not from money, and she turns to collective action first.
Says she would learn one AI tool only to catch its mistakes, which fits her resistance.

steps.text: Join the graduate branch of the engineers' union in January
Ask Dr Weiss for a place on his bridge-monitoring project
Try one load-check tool to learn where it fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not just a tech story. Governments need to slow it down or at least guarantee support, and I'd be at every march. I'd write to my member of parliament that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. Two years means I graduate into a market where firms have just discovered the software does my job, and the building robots come around 2031. The thinking side of structural design could go first, and I'm the slow one in my group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, since it's paid for, and go to the union's emergency meeting. I'd ask my parents to keep funding me an extra year if needed. I'd also finally sit down with a chatbot for an hour a day, hating every minute, because refusing seems silly now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a tight chest. I still feel I have some control, because my parents' money gives me a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that Chen's Pharmacy might matter more than my degree, and I might help out there for a while. I'd say it as a joke, but I'd mean half of it. Mum would hate it, and she'd also be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change what you do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd hold more cash and not spend on a flat deposit, because I wouldn't know what job I'd have. I'd keep every penny of the six months and ask my parents to hold off their own plans to expand the pharmacy.

say: This is a **political emergency**, and governments must guarantee support.
I'd write to my member of parliament that week.
think: I'd be frightened: I graduate just as firms find the software **does my job**.
I'm the slowest in my group on AI, which makes me feel **behind**.
do: Finish the master's, join the union's **emergency meeting** and march.
Spend an hour a day on a **chatbot**, hating it but doing it.
feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, but cushioned by **family money**.
S2.quote: Chen's Pharmacy might matter more than my degree, and I might help out there for a while.
fieldNote: Her resistance cracks here: she agrees to **try AI** daily, which she refuses in milder worlds.
Falls back on the **family pharmacy** as a plan B, half joking and half serious.

steps.text: Attend the union's emergency meeting and join the march
Write to my member of parliament about guaranteed support
Practise with a chatbot for an hour every evening
Help at the family pharmacy while the market settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not enough to retrain a country, and the unions and the government should start now. At university I'd tell friends to learn something hands-on as a backup. Online I'd stay quiet, since people just argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have a first job for two or three years before it bites. Then the thinking tasks go and the robots arrive around 2034, which touches site work too. I'm anxious, but less than in the two-year world, because I'd have time to get real experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a graduate post in a smaller firm where I'm on site often, and save most of my salary. I'd join the union at once and put money into a flat deposit only after two years. I'd also learn the basic software tools in the first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. The three years feel like a window I can use if I don't waste them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with three more years than in the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first two years of experience are what I'd be buying. I'd pick a firm with a good site engineer, a man called Mr Okafor in my imagination, someone who teaches. If robots arrive in 2034, I'd want to be the person who knows what the robot should be doing, not the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to guide you through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My union rep, honestly, and my supervisor Dr Weiss. I wouldn't trust a company's careers page or a minister's speech. I trust people who've had to fix real buildings.

say: Five years is **not enough** to retrain a country, so start now.
I'd tell friends to learn something **hands-on** as a backup.
think: I'd get **two or three years** in a job before the thinking tasks go.
Robots around 2034 reach **site work** too, so experience has to be the real kind.
do: Take a graduate post at a small firm where I'm on **site** often.
Save most of my salary and **delay** a flat deposit for two years.
feel: Anxious but steadier, treating the extra years as a **window**.
S3.quote: I'd want to be the person who knows what the robot should be doing, not the person it replaces.
fieldNote: She reasons about **hands-on versus desk** work, and picks site experience over desk work.
Trust goes to people who have fixed real buildings, not to firms or ministers.

steps.text: Take a graduate post at a small firm with site visits
Save most of the first salary for two years
Join the engineers' union in the first week
Learn the basic design software tools on the job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should use it for good rules and retraining funds. I'd say it at the union and in my student paper, and I'd back anyone who stands on that platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's still scary but manageable. I'd be thirty-four by 2036, with eight or nine years of experience, maybe a chartered engineer, and a lot of what I'd do would be judgement and sign-off. I think the people who can sign a drawing are the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, get a first job, and work towards chartership as fast as possible. I'd save a house deposit and I'd vote for any party with a retraining plan. I'd learn the AI tools slowly over a few years, since I'm not in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, no more. It feels like weather far off, and I'm in no rush to change my coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the decade, if you could plan it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick chartership, because a signature carries legal weight and firms need a human to carry it. I'd study for the professional exam while working. In ten years I might also run a small practice with my friend Aiko.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you expect your parents to stand in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would be sixty-something by then, and the pharmacy might have a robot dispenser and a smaller team. They'd probably still be working. I'd want to make sure they have a pension, and not just rely on me.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and we should use it for rules and retraining funds.
I'd back any party with a clear **retraining plan**.
think: By 2036 I'd have years of experience, and **signing drawings** is judgement that stays human longer.
It's still scary, but I'm in **no rush** to change anything.
do: Work towards **chartership** while holding my first job.
Save a **house deposit** and learn AI tools slowly over a few years.
feel: Uneasy and no more, like **weather** a long way off.
S4.quote: I think the people who can sign a drawing are the last to go.
fieldNote: The long runway lets her **keep her habits**: slow tool learning, union politics, chartership.
Her calm depends on one belief, that **legal sign-off** stays with people.

steps.text: Study for the chartership exam while in the first job
Save a house deposit from the graduate salary
Vote for the party with a retraining plan
Learn one AI design tool each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have no time to get experience, and my average degree and no internship would count against me. What would help is guaranteed support, like a graduate retraining fund, and a union that bargains for entry-level jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I don't think so. I'd just say that we shouldn't treat people who are slow with technology as stubborn. I'm careful, and careful people checked bridges before there was software.

headlineQuote: I'm careful, and careful people checked bridges before there was software.
portrait: Olga is a **24-year-old** master's student in structural engineering, with no debt and parents who pay her fees.
She passed her bachelor's with an average result and **no internship**, and that gap shapes her worries.
She is progressive and union-minded, and she is **resistant** to new tools until a crisis forces her hand.
Her mood rises from calm in the mild world to **anxious** in the two- and five-year worlds.
Her fallbacks are the family pharmacy, union support and slow, **hands-on** experience.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most, because she would graduate with no experience and an average degree.
whatWouldHelp: A graduate **retraining fund** and a union that bargains for entry-level jobs.
